title: AI Memory Gap at DAC 2026 - Semiwiki
gist: At a Synopsys exhibitor session during DAC 2026, startups TetraMem (ReRAM crossbar in-memory compute) and ANAFLASH (Flash-based Reflex Computing Unit and Legato-Logic) pitched computing directly inside non-volatile memory as a power-efficient alternative to HBM-centric AI hardware for edge use cases like wearables, with both relying on Synopsys Cloud to reach tape-out without hiring dedicated CAD/IT teams.

themes.theme: In-memory compute as an HBM alternative for edge AI

insights.claim: TetraMem and ANAFLASH compute directly inside non-volatile memory instead of moving data between memory and processor, positioning in-memory compute as a lower-power architectural alternative to the HBM-heavy data movement pattern used in AI datacenter hardware.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Watch in-memory-compute startups as a potential edge-AI alternative to HBM-centric architectures, though the near-term addressable market described here is edge devices, not datacenter AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: Datacenters consume large amounts of HBM chips in their AI hardware systems, but these two companies are taking a different approach by computing directly inside non-volatile memory, avoiding the power-hungry step of moving data between memory and processor.

insights.claim: The author concludes that always-on, low-power edge AI use cases—not datacenter-scale AI—are the near-term commercial proof point where in-memory-compute architectures already fit market requirements.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic near-term revenue expectation for IMC vendors: edge/wearable markets first, not hyperscaler AI infrastructure, which should temper aggressive TAM assumptions.
insights.quote: I was impressed with the in-memory approaches that these two companies delivered to the market for edge AI cases. There are many commercial uses where always-on capabilities and low-power efficiency dominate the requirements

insights.claim: TetraMem, founded in 2018, shipped its first multi-level ReRAM in-memory-compute chip in 2026 and holds over 120 patents protecting the technology, with more than 10 silicon tape-outs already using its IMC.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: A 120-patent portfolio plus 10-plus tape-outs signals a real IP moat and customer traction beyond a lab demo, relevant to any IP-licensing or acquisition thesis around ReRAM in-memory compute.
insights.quote: his company started in 2018, with their first multi-level ReRAM chip for In Memory Compute (IMC) shipping in 2026, protected by over 120 patents. There are already over 10 silicon tape-outs so far using their IMC.

insights.claim: TetraMem's multi-level RRAM stores up to 11 bits per cell and programs AI weights directly into the array, performing the multiply-accumulate operation in place and eliminating the high-bandwidth IO bottleneck that constrains conventional memory-processor architectures.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Bits-per-cell density is the key technical lever determining TetraMem's area/power advantage versus digital SRAM- or HBM-based accelerators; track roadmap progress on this metric as a proxy for competitiveness.
insights.quote: Using multi-level resistive random-access memory (RRAM) allows precision programming with up to 11 bit/cell, making for a smaller area and power compared to digital memory.

insights.claim: TetraMem's MLX200 chip pairs a RISC-V CPU with an analog in-memory-compute NPU macro on a 22nm process, targeting wearable health devices that need voice detection, always-on wake, and keyword spotting.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Names a concrete, near-term commercial market (wearable health) rather than a speculative datacenter thesis, useful for sizing TetraMem's initial revenue opportunity.
insights.quote: An example chip called the MLX200 used a 22nm process for Edge-AI acceleration, which had a RISC-V CPU coupled with an analog IMC NPU macro, along with integrated audio and peripheral blocks.

insights.claim: ANAFLASH's Reflex Computing Unit mimics sensory and motor neuron behavior using nonvolatile compute coupled with FLASH memory, aiming to eliminate AI model data traffic entirely rather than merely reduce it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Represents a fundamentally different circuit philosophy (neuromorphic-style, Flash-based) from TetraMem's ReRAM crossbar, giving investors two distinct technical bets to compare within the same in-memory-compute theme.
insights.quote: their Reflex Computing Unit that mimics the behavior of sensory neurons and motor neurons by using nonvolatile AI computing technology coupled with FLASH memory. This approach eliminates AI model traffic.
insights.locator: paragraph introducing ANAFLASH / R. Scott Hills

insights.claim: ANAFLASH's second chip, Legato-Logic, is a time-domain Neural Network Processor built from standard logic that integrates into any type of memory, enabling low-power, low-latency execution of large AI models where they are stored.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Compatibility with standard logic (versus an exotic RRAM process) could mean faster foundry portability and lower integration risk than TetraMem's crossbar approach.
insights.quote: Legato-Logic uses standard logic and a time-domain compute-in-memory technology that integrates into any type of memory, reducing data traffic between processor and memory.

insights.claim: ANAFLASH cited resource constraints, a globally distributed design team, and a preference for well-established IP as its key product-development challenges under schedule pressure.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Illustrates the resource limits a small fabless AI-silicon startup faces, context for evaluating how quickly such teams can scale from tape-out to production.
insights.quote: Challenges at ANAFLASH were resource constraints under the product development schedule, a global design team, and the desire to use well-established IP.

themes.theme: Synopsys Cloud as enabler for fabless AI-silicon startups

insights.claim: TetraMem used Synopsys Cloud to achieve system bring-up in minutes and speed RTL verification simulation without hiring additional CAD engineers or building IT infrastructure, lowering the capital and headcount barrier for a small IMC startup to reach tape-out.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Cloud EDA lowering the fixed cost of chip design could accelerate the number of niche AI-silicon startups reaching production, a tailwind for Synopsys Cloud adoption and a data point for the broader EDA-as-a-service thesis.
insights.quote: TetraMem used Synopsys Cloud in their workflow to provide quick system bring-up in just minutes, avoid unexpected down time, experience little maintenance time, and speed Register Transfer Level (RTL) verification simulation, all without additional CAD engineers and IT infrastructure resources.

insights.claim: Both TetraMem and ANAFLASH used Synopsys Cloud to bring their in-memory-compute chips to market without their design teams needing to hire extra CAD and IT engineers to support EDA infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: A repeated pattern across two independent startups strengthens the case that Synopsys Cloud is becoming a default infrastructure choice for capital-constrained AI-silicon startups, worth monitoring for further design-win disclosures.
insights.quote: These companies also used Synopsys Cloud to get their products to market without their design teams needing to hire extra CAD and IT engineers to support an EDA infrastructure.
